title: In-situ Characterization of Dust Nodules in Ice Cores from the Tibetan Plateau
content: Mineral dust is the largest emission by mass into the atmosphere and these particles affect the radiation balance through direct and indirect effects including scattering, cloud nuclei, and heterogeneous chemistry [1]. Glacial ice cores give valuable insight to understand previous emission cycles and events [2]. There have been many studies to characterize particles in ice cores, however, because the samples are often melted before analysis, valuable information regarding the orientation and arrangement of particles, and soluble chemistry of those particles within the ice is lost. For example, while it has been reported that the deep layers of ice cores from the Tibetan Plateau contain unusual clay nodules [3], the structure of these nodules in-situ is poorly understood. In this study we aim to observe the interaction of particles trapped in their native environment to understand the nodule formation and effects on the surrounding ice.
